job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Diego Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now my day is a mix of couch and laptop in the rented flat I share with my friend Kenji in Sheffield. I finished a software engineering degree in June with a plain pass. My final project was a booking site for a community bike co-op, and it half works. I apply to a few jobs each morning, then go for a long run, then spend the afternoon on a small game I'm making so I'm doing something that isn't rejection emails.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you at it on the bad days?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mum is a nurse and she's in her union, so at dinner she tells me every job should have a rep. Dad is quieter and just sends me links to vacancies. I've never done an internship, which sounds like a small gap, but it's the first thing recruiters ask about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, so the market might stop wobbling. At the pub I'd probably joke that I can finally stop reading AI news. Online I wouldn't say a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately my problem is the same. No offer, no internship, and a pass doesn't stand out among 300 other applicants. There are plenty of openings in Sheffield, so I do think I'll land something by spring, but I wouldn't bet my rent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep up the morning applications and ask Kenji's cousin, who works at a logistics firm, for an intro. I'd put two small projects on my GitHub with proper write-ups. And I'd use an AI helper for explaining stack traces now and then, as I do already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. A bit restless, like waiting for a train that's late but definitely coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd land something by spring but wouldn't bet your rent. What's the gap there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have savings for about eight months, and my parents would help. So I'm not betting rent, I'm betting my pride. If spring comes and nothing happens, that's when it gets weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the two small projects would you put first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bike co-op booking site. It has real users, about 40 members, and one of them left me a nice message. A real person using it beats any tutorial clone.

say: I'd joke at the pub that I can **stop reading** AI news.
Online I'd say nothing; I don't post about work.
think: My real problem is **no offer** and no internship among 300 other applicants.
Plenty of openings in Sheffield, so I expect something by **spring**.
do: Keep up **morning applications** and ask Kenji's cousin at a logistics firm for an intro.
Add two small projects to **GitHub** with proper write-ups.
feel: **Restless**, like waiting for a late train that will come.
S0.quote: I'm not betting rent, I'm betting my pride. If spring comes and nothing happens, that's when it gets weird.
fieldNote: He reads **pride** as the real stake, since his savings and parents cover rent.
Already uses AI **lightly**, so the plateau changes little for him.
Real users of his co-op site are his best **evidence**.

steps.text: Send three applications every morning to Sheffield software firms
Ask Kenji's cousin for an intro at the logistics firm
Use an AI helper to explain stack traces while coding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the thing everyone in my course keeps whispering about: the grad coding job is the first rung getting sawn off. I'd say workers should have a voice in how it's rolled out. My mum would say, get a union, and she'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think coding, writing and checking are exactly what AI takes over. A firm that hired five juniors now hires two and gives them the AI tool. I'm one of 300 applicants for two seats. And I'm a pass with no internship, so I'd be among the first cut from any shortlist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retarget. Not just coding roles but support engineer, QA and systems admin, where a person still talks to people. I'd do a cloud certificate in the first six months, about 300 pounds, and join a local tech workers' group so someone I know can vouch for me. I'd also take a short contract before a perfect job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a working way. It makes me move. If I felt calm I'd probably drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a union. What would a union do for someone with no job yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe nothing directly, but it'd shape the rules. Like making firms say if they replaced juniors with software, or fund retraining. I'd also like a place where juniors can compare notes on what firms are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your steadiness about AI tools come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use them a bit, but I wait until it's proven. I don't want to be the first to trust something. I want a few people I know to have used it for six months without disaster.

say: I'd say the **first rung** of the graduate ladder is being sawn off.
I'd say workers need a **voice** in how AI is rolled out.
think: Firms will hire **two juniors**, and I'd be one of 300 for two seats.
With a pass and no internship I'm **easy to cut** from a shortlist.
do: Apply for **QA and support engineer** roles as well as plain coding jobs.
Do a **cloud certificate** in six months and join a local tech workers' group.
feel: **Anxious** in a way that makes me move; calm would make me drift.
S1.quote: A firm that hired five juniors now hires two and gives them the AI tool. I'm one of 300 applicants for two seats.
fieldNote: Identifies **desk-based** entry roles as the exposed ones.
Moves toward **people-facing** roles and a short contract.
His steadiness shows: he wants **proof** from peers before trusting tools.

steps.text: Apply for QA, support engineer and systems admin roles
Finish a cloud certificate costing about 300 pounds
Join a local tech workers' group and go to monthly meetups
Take on small freelance fixes for the bike co-op and others

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a pause on release dates and a seat at the table for workers. Two years isn't enough for any society. I'd turn up to a protest if one was organised, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think a lot of my field goes first. Coding is the thing AI does well, and by 2028 a junior like me is just a cost on a spreadsheet. Robots take three more years for hands-on work, so a plumber or electrician has until about 2031. I don't have a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job that gets me through the door and into a company with a union, even a support desk. I'd start training in a trade-adjacent field, like building services or electrical installation, because the hands-on route lasts a few years longer. I'd keep my eight months of savings untouched and ask my parents about moving back home to save rent. And I'd tell Kenji we may need to split the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit sick. Not panic, because I have savings and a plan, but there's a pit in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at a trade. What do you imagine that day looks like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold mornings, a van, a lot of crawl spaces. Weirdly I'm okay with it. I'd rather be useful with my hands than be a coder with no work, and my uncle already does installations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kenji about splitting the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not about us, it's about runway. If I move home for a year I can save about 6,000 and still have a bed to come back to. He'd probably do the same.

say: I'd call for a **pause** on release dates and a seat for workers.
I'd go to my first **protest** if one was organised.
think: By 2028 a junior coder is just a **cost on a spreadsheet**.
Robots take three more years, so **hands-on work** lasts longer than mine.
do: Take **any job** with a company that has a union, even a support desk.
Train in **electrical installation** with my uncle's firm, and move home to save.
feel: **Anxious** with a pit in my stomach, but I have savings and a plan.
S2.quote: I'd rather be useful with my hands than be a coder with no work, and my uncle already does installations.
fieldNote: Switches from desk to **trade** thinking faster than most, in line with his steadiness.
Savings and family create **runway**, so anxiety stays short of alarm.

steps.text: Take any support desk job at a firm with a union
Start an electrical installation course with my uncle's firm
Move back home and save about 6,000 in a year
Join the first organised protest on AI release dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do this properly, which is rare. Make firms report when AI replaces jobs, tax the gains, fund retraining. I'd say it at every dinner until my uncle gets annoyed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the first one where I can plan. Five years is long enough to get a job, learn the craft, and be someone with experience before it hits. Robots for hands-on work would be around 2034, so even the trade route stays open. I'd feel almost lucky if I use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get any software job within the year and treat it as school. I'd learn from seniors how things actually break, because that's what AI won't do as well. I'd also build up a small cushion, 300 a month, and use evenings to do a part-time master's or an electrical short course just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. I don't love that it's a plan made out of fear, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plan is made of fear. Is that bad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not bad, just honest. Fear has made me do more this year than excitement ever did. I'd rather admit it than pretend I'm into hustle culture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want from the firm that takes you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real mentor and a written plan for the first year. I'd even take lower pay for it. If a firm gives me a senior who actually explains things, I'd stay.

say: I'd say firms should **report** when AI replaces jobs and fund retraining.
I'd keep saying it at dinner until my uncle gets annoyed.
think: Five years is enough to be someone with **experience** before it hits.
The trade route stays open until about **2034**.
do: Land **any software job** in the year and learn from seniors how things break.
Save **300 a month** and take a part-time course in evenings.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**: a plan made from fear is still a plan.
S3.quote: Fear has made me do more this year than excitement ever did. I'd rather admit it than pretend I'm into hustle culture.
fieldNote: He treats the five-year window as the first **plannable** scenario.
Wants a **mentor** more than money, which echoes his current gap.

steps.text: Accept any software job within the first year
Save 300 a month from the first pay
Take an evening electrical short course as a backup
Push firms to report AI job replacement through my union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance to get it right. I'd tell friends to stay informed and to vote. At home I'd say it's the first time I've felt the future was negotiable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's almost calm. A decade lets me get a job, change jobs, probably become the person who understands the thing, and have enough saved to survive a bad year. If AGI arrives in 2036, I'm 33. That's young enough to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year is the same as always: find any entry job, ideally in a firm with a union, and save. Then I'd aim at jobs where I explain technology to people, like technical support leadership or training. I'd also do a degree top-up in something regulated, maybe safety engineering, over five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with a small wobble when I picture 2036. I'd probably still check the news too often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be 33. What would you want to have by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A home of my own that isn't mortgaged to the hilt. A job where my name is on something. And maybe someone to share it with. Saying it out loud sounds too normal, but that's the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with the calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If nothing happens in the first three years and everyone relaxes. The decade can be wasted. I'd want checkpoints, like yearly public reviews of what jobs changed.

say: I'd say ten years is a **chance** to get it right.
I'd tell friends to stay informed and **vote**.
think: A decade is enough to learn, change jobs and **save**.
At 33, I'd be young enough to **start again**.
do: Find an **entry job** at a firm with a union, and save.
Study safety engineering part-time over **five years**.
feel: **Calm**, with a small wobble when I picture 2036.
S4.quote: If AGI arrives in 2036, I'm 33. That's young enough to start again.
fieldNote: The **longest** horizon is the only one where he feels calm.
He wants public **checkpoints** to stop a wasted decade.
Imagines a plain **future**: home, name on a project, someone to share it.

steps.text: Find an entry job at a unionised firm
Save a fixed amount each month toward a deposit
Study safety engineering part-time over five years
Vote for candidates who back public yearly reviews of AI job changes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. I'd have the least time, and I'd have to pivot with no experience. What would help is a public safety net that kicks in before you lose out, plus a junior programme where firms must take a few trainees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people my age aren't asking for handouts. We're asking for a first chance and a fair set of rules. I did not expect to be this serious today.

headlineQuote: People my age aren't asking for handouts. We're asking for a first chance and a fair set of rules.
portrait: Diego is **23**, a software engineering graduate with a plain pass, sharing a rented flat in Sheffield and applying for work.
He is progressive, backs **unions and rules**, and talks like his nurse mother, with dry humour and little drama.
He is a steady adopter: he uses AI **now and then** and wants proof from people he trusts before leaning on it.
His savings give him **runway**, so he moves from uneasy to anxious, and only calm with ten years.
His plan B is a **hands-on trade** through his uncle's electrical firm, which he starts to find appealing.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most because a junior coder would have no time to build experience.
whatWouldHelp: A **safety net** that starts before people lose out, plus a junior programme where firms must take trainees.
